0.badge: 1 • WELCOMING THE MOMENT • WISHING FOR A CHILD

1.title: A question. A flutter. A possibility.

p.1:
Sometimes the wish for a child arrives without warning.

Sometimes it has been there for a long time, taking us back to our own childhood.

Sometimes it slips in gently, almost without a sound.
p.2:
It can be clear or blurry.

Sometimes shared, sometimes carried more by one of the two.

It can live alongside joy, questions, fears or a great deal of hesitation.
p.3: There is no single way to wish for a child.
p.4: This wish is woven from what we have lived, what we carry within us, what we hope for… and also what worries us.
p.5:
This is not the place to decide or settle anything.

This Carnet is not waiting for an answer.

It simply offers a quiet space to listen to what is there — even if it is fragile, contradictory or still without words.
p.6: Giving this wish a place — or its absence — is already a way of taking care of yourself.

1.quote: A wish can begin with a thought, a feeling… or simply a question.

2.intro:
Naming a hesitation does not cancel the wish.

Listening to what you feel already gives it a place.
2.quote: Even before a story begins, something may already be starting to move.

4.title: The first imagined names

p.1: Talking about a name can be one of the first moments when a child who is still imaginary begins to take a place in our thoughts.
p.2: This is not yet about making a final choice.
p.3: Alone or together, let the names come: the ones you like, the ones that bring something to mind, the ones from your family history or, on the contrary, the ones that open onto something new.
p.4:
One name may be spoken with enthusiasm.

Another dropped a few days later.

Some may come back over time.
p.5: What matters here is not the final choice, but keeping a trace of these first imagined names.

p.1: The wish for a child can come with contradictory feelings: joy and eagerness, but also doubts, hesitations or worries.
p.2: Donald Winnicott (1896–1971) – British paediatrician and psychoanalyst, specialist in early emotional development and the parent–child relationship.
p.3: Winnicott’s work lets us think about parenthood without requiring parents to be perfectly sure, available or free of all ambivalence. Becoming a parent also involves inner reshaping and a gradual adjustment to a new reality.
p.4: So hesitation does not necessarily mean the wish is not real. It can also reflect what the possible arrival of a child stands for: responsibilities, life changes, changes in the couple, or questions about one’s own ability to become a parent.
p.5: Recognising these feelings makes it possible to hear them without having to resolve them straight away.

points.1: The wish for a child can exist alongside doubts or worries.
points.2: Ambivalence does not necessarily mean there is no wish.
points.3: Becoming a parent brings personal, couple and family changes.
points.4: You don’t need an immediate answer to every question.
points.5: Putting words to what you feel can already help you understand what is at play.

p.1: Long before any birth, a child can already begin to exist in the imagination.
p.2:
Sometimes a face is imagined.

A personality.

A name.

A resemblance.

A future relationship.
p.3: Serge Lebovici (1915–2000) – French psychiatrist, psychoanalyst and child psychiatrist, specialist in early interactions between parents and children.
p.4: Lebovici worked in particular on the images parents build around the child, and on how their own inner history shapes those images.
p.5: This imagined child is, of course, not yet the real child.
p.6: If a child comes, meeting them will gradually reveal a unique person, with their own temperament, needs and way of relating to others.
p.7: Moving from the imagined child to the real child then calls for adjustments: some images fade, others change.

points.1: A child can begin to be imagined long before birth.
points.2: These images can be about appearance, personality, name or the future relationship.
points.3: The imagined child is also shaped by the adult’s history and expectations.
points.4: The real child will never exactly match the imagined child.
points.5: The relationship is built gradually, by discovering the child as they are.

p.1: Wishing for a child can also reawaken your own story.
p.2:
Memories come back.

Family patterns show up.

Some things make you want to pass them on.

Others make you want to do things differently.
p.3: Françoise Dolto (1908–1988) – French paediatrician and psychoanalyst, best known for her work on childhood, speech and the child’s place in the family story.
p.4: Dolto’s thinking gives an important place to how a child is written into a family story and to what passes between generations, notably through words, things left unsaid and family images.
p.5: Becoming a parent can therefore lead you to revisit your own childhood: what you received, what was missing, what you want to pass on and what you would like to live differently.
p.6: Recognising this story does not mean being bound by it.
p.7: It can become a starting point from which a new relationship can be built.

points.1: The wish for a child can reawaken memories of your own childhood.
points.2: A family story passes on values, patterns and images.
points.3: Some of what is passed on is conscious, some much less so.
points.4: Recognising what you received also helps you think about what you want to change.
points.5: A new child joins a family story while opening a new one.

closing.1: One day, you were only a dream. And yet you already had a place in my heart.
